title: Kernels: The Geometry of Learning
subtitle: A book-form synthesis of the kernel-methods literature
source: This book synthesizes three standard sources: the lecture course "Machine Learning with Kernel Methods" by Julien Mairal and Jean-Philippe Vert (kernel-learning.github.io), and the textbooks "Learning with Kernels" by Bernhard Schölkopf and Alexander Smola (2002) and "Kernel Methods for Pattern Analysis" by John Shawe-Taylor and Nello Cristianini (2004). All results and their attributions follow these sources; the connecting prose, the pedagogical arc, and the interactive figures are this book's.

parts.intro: A self-contained reference for the mathematics the book leans on, drawn from linear algebra, analysis and Hilbert spaces, probability, optimization, and functional analysis. Read it front to back for a refresher, or dip in when a later chapter cites a result by name.

Kernel methods rest on one move: compare examples with a similarity function, and a surprising amount of learning follows. This part builds the idea from the ground up, from the definition of a valid similarity to the space it secretly defines and the theorem that makes computation possible.

chapters.title: The Kernel Trick and the Representer Theorem

parts.part: II · Supervised Machines with a Fixed Kernel
parts.intro: Fix a kernel and a supervised task. This part derives the workhorse algorithms as one recipe under different loss functions: ridge regression and the support vector machine for classification, the epsilon-insensitive machine for regression, the one-class machine for novelty, and the pairwise machine for ranking.

chapters.title: Kernel Ridge Regression and Smooth Losses

parts.intro: A kernel machine is only as useful as the solver behind it. This part opens the quadratic program the dual defines and builds the algorithms that make it tractable at scale, from decomposition and sequential minimal optimization to online updates that never store the whole Gram matrix.

chapters.title: Solving the SVM: Decomposition and SMO

parts.intro: Why should a machine fit on a sample predict on the unseen? This part answers with two lineages: the modern Rademacher and margin bounds for RKHS balls, and the classical VC and structural-risk theory that framed the field, each turning a capacity measure into a guarantee.

The same Gram matrix that drives supervised learning drives the unsupervised kind. Kernel PCA, clustering, canonical correlation, the supervised discriminants, and multidimensional scaling are one family of subspace methods, each a generalized eigenproblem or deflation read through the kernel.

parts.part: VI · The Geometry of the Space
parts.intro: Why did any of it work? This part opens the RKHS with Mercer's theorem, reads its spectrum as a measure of smoothness, and turns eigenvalue decay into concrete rates of convergence.

Everything so far assumed a kernel was handed to you. This part builds them: for vectors by symmetry and probability, for prior knowledge through invariance, for the structured data (sequences, text, graphs) where the kernel is the only bridge to the RKHS toolbox, for paths and time series, for curved and symmetric domains, and even for the indefinite similarities that fall outside the positive-definite world.

A kernel can embed not just a point but an entire probability distribution. This part builds the mean embedding, tests whether two samples come from the same law, measures distributions by the distance between embeddings and by optimal transport, and integrates against them with kernel quadrature.

chapters.title: Mean Embeddings, MMD, and Characteristic Kernels

parts.intro: Embeddings turn probability into linear algebra, and that opens inference. This part embeds conditional distributions as operators, tests goodness of fit against an unnormalized model with a Stein operator, reads causal questions through the RKHS, and learns when the training example is itself a distribution.

chapters.title: Conditional Mean Embeddings and Kernel Bayes' Rule
Kernel Stein Discrepancy and Stein Methods

parts.part: X · Scaling and Learning the Kernel
parts.intro: The exact solve does not survive a million examples, and the kernel need not be fixed or shallow. This part removes the quadratic wall, learns the kernel itself, and reads deep networks as kernel machines.

chapters.title: Deep Learning from a Kernel Point of View

parts.intro: The same kernel that defines a norm defines a covariance. This part reads kernel ridge regression as the posterior mean of a Gaussian process, develops inference and hyperparameter learning, reaches the sparse Bayesian machines that put a probability on every prediction, and turns that uncertainty into a rule for what to measure next.

The two standard textbooks close around 2004, before the deep-learning era rewrote what kernels are for. This part is a guide to what came after: the interpolation revolution that revised the book's own theory of generalization, and the frontier where fixed kernels give way to learned features.

chapters.title: The Frontier: Feature Learning and Beyond

parts.intro: Theory meets the terminal. This closing part walks end-to-end applications, the model-selection and implementation choices that decide whether a kernel method works in practice, and a map of the software that puts these methods a few lines of code away.
